units.title: Hello, PHP!
units.summary: Write your first PHP script, print text and numbers with echo, and learn why every statement ends with a semicolon.

lesson.md: PHP is a programming language for websites and scripts. A PHP file starts with the tag `<?php`. Everything after it is PHP code. The command `echo` prints text, and every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.

lesson.code:
<?php
echo "Hello, PHP!";

lesson.md: Line by line: `<?php` tells PHP that the code begins here. `echo` prints the value after it. The text between the double quotes is a **string**, which means a piece of text. The semicolon `;` ends the statement, like a full stop ends a sentence.

`echo` does not start a new line by itself. Inside double quotes, `\n` stands for a new line. You can also give `echo` several values separated by commas. It prints them one after the other, without spaces in between.

lesson.code:
<?php
echo "One";
echo "Two\n";
echo "A", "B", "C", "\n";
echo "Done\n";

lesson.md: PHP can calculate for you. Numbers are written without quotes. Use `+` to add, `-` to subtract, `*` to multiply and `/` to divide. `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is only text.

lesson.code:
<?php
echo 2 + 3, "\n";
echo "2 + 3\n";
echo 7 * 6, "\n";
echo 10 / 4, "\n";

lesson.md: You can also write strings in single quotes, like `'Hello'`. PHP prints single-quoted strings exactly as they are written. So `'\n'` is a backslash and the letter `n`, not a new line. Use double quotes when you need `\n`.

lesson.code:
<?php
echo 'Hello\n';
echo "\n";
echo "Hello\n";

lesson.md: To run a script, save it in a file such as `hello.php` and type `php hello.php` in a terminal. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and PHP ignores it. In the exercises, short examples often leave out the `<?php` line.

If you forget a semicolon, PHP stops with a **parse error** and does not run any line of the script. The error message names the line where PHP noticed the problem, which is often the line after the missing `;`.

card: `echo "Hi\n";` prints text, `\n` starts a new line
`'\n'` in single quotes is not a new line

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, get to know int, float, string and bool, and look at them with var_dump and gettype.

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name, so you can use it later. In PHP, every variable name starts with a dollar sign `$`. The equals sign `=` puts the value on the right into the variable on the left.

lesson.code:
<?php
$name = "Ada";
$age = 36;
echo $name, "\n";
echo $age, "\n";
$age = 37;
echo $age, "\n";

lesson.md: A variable can get a new value at any time: `$age = 37;` replaces `36`. After the `$`, a name starts with a letter or an underscore `_`. Names are case sensitive, so `$age` and `$Age` are two different variables. For names with several words, write `$firstName`.

Every value has a **type**. An `int` is a whole number like `42`. A `float` is a number with a decimal point like `9.99`. A `string` is text like `"Paris"`. A `bool` is either `true` or `false`. PHP sees the type from the value, so you do not write it yourself.
The function `var_dump` shows the type and the value of a variable. For a string, it also shows the number of characters. This is very useful when you want to know what a variable holds.

lesson.code:
<?php
$count = 42;
$price = 9.99;
$city = "Paris";
$open = true;
var_dump($count);
var_dump($price);
var_dump($city);
var_dump($open);

lesson.md: The function `gettype` returns the name of the type as a string. Note that it calls a float `double` and a bool `boolean`, for historical reasons.

lesson.code:
<?php
echo gettype(42), "\n";
echo gettype(1.5), "\n";
echo gettype("hi"), "\n";
echo gettype(false), "\n";

lesson.md: Besides `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, there is `%` for the remainder of a division and `**` for powers. `/` gives a float when the result is not whole; `intdiv` divides and keeps only the whole part. `$a += 10` is short for `$a = $a + 10`, and `$b++` adds 1 to `$b`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$a = 7;
$b = 2;
echo $a + $b, "\n";
echo $a / $b, "\n";
echo intdiv($a, $b), "\n";
echo $a % $b, "\n";
echo $a ** $b, "\n";
$a += 10;
echo $a, "\n";
$b++;
echo $b, "\n";

lesson.md: `echo` prints `true` as `1` and `false` as nothing at all. When you want to see what a variable really holds, use `var_dump`.

units.title: Working with strings
units.summary: Join strings with the dot, put variables into text, and use strlen, strtoupper, str_replace and substr.

lesson.md: To join two strings, PHP uses the dot `.` as an operator. This is called **concatenation**. PHP does not use `+` for this. `.=` adds text to the end of a variable.

lesson.code:
<?php
$first = "Ada";
$last = "Lovelace";
$full = $first . " " . $last;
echo $full . "\n";
echo "Age: " . 36 . "\n";
$text = "Hello";
$text .= ", World!";
echo $text . "\n";

lesson.md: In double quotes, PHP replaces a variable with its value. This is called **interpolation**. In single quotes, PHP does not do this and prints the name with the `$`.
When letters follow the variable name directly, put curly braces around the variable: `{$fruit}s`. Without them, PHP would look for a variable called `$fruits`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$name = "Ada";
$count = 3;
$fruit = "apple";
echo "Hi $name!\n";
echo 'Hi $name!' . "\n";
echo "You have $count new messages.\n";
echo "Two {$fruit}s\n";
lesson.output:
Hi Ada!
Hi $name!
You have 3 new messages.
Two apples

lesson.md: PHP has many functions for strings. `strlen` counts the characters. `strtoupper` changes all letters to capital letters, and `strtolower` to small letters. `str_replace` takes three values: what to search for, what to put instead, and the string to change.

lesson.code:
<?php
$word = "banana";
echo strlen($word), "\n";
echo strtoupper($word), "\n";
echo strtolower("HeLLo"), "\n";
echo str_replace("a", "o", $word), "\n";

lesson.md: `substr` cuts out a part of a string. The positions of the characters are counted from `0`, not from `1`. `substr($s, 0, 4)` returns 4 characters starting at position `0`. Without a length, it goes to the end. A negative start counts from the end. `$s[0]` returns the character at position `0`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$language = "JavaScript";
echo substr($language, 0, 4), "\n";
echo substr($language, 4), "\n";
echo substr($language, -3), "\n";
echo $language[0], "\n";

lesson.md: `+` always calculates. `"5" + "3"` gives the number `8`, but `"5" . "3"` gives the string `"53"`. With text that is not a number, like `"Hi" + "Ada"`, PHP stops with an error.
`strlen` counts bytes. Letters such as `é` or `ü` take two bytes, so `strlen("é")` is `2`. For English letters, digits and spaces, one character is one byte.

card: `substr($s, 0, 3)` cuts out a part, positions start at `0`

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your code decide with if, elseif and else, compare with == and ===, combine conditions and pick values with match.

lesson.md: Comparisons give a bool: `true` or `false`. You compare with `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less or equal), `>=` (greater or equal), `===` (equal) and `!==` (not equal).

`if` runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses `( )`, the block in curly braces `{ }`. `elseif` checks another condition, and `else` runs when no condition was `true`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$temperature = 25;
if ($temperature > 30) {
    echo "Hot\n";
} elseif ($temperature > 20) {
    echo "Warm\n";
} else {
    echo "Cold\n";
}

lesson.md: PHP checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`. Here `25 > 30` is `false`, but `25 > 20` is `true`, so PHP prints `Warm` and skips the rest.

PHP has two ways to test if values are equal. `==` (loose) converts the types first, so the string `"5"` and the int `5` count as equal. `===` (strict) also checks the type. The opposites are `!=` and `!==`. Use `===` and `!==` whenever you can, because they hold fewer surprises.

lesson.code:
<?php
var_dump("5" == 5);
var_dump("5" === 5);
var_dump(5 === 5);
var_dump(5 !== 5.0);

lesson.md: You can combine conditions with **logical operators**. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and the other way round.

lesson.code:
<?php
$age = 70;
$hasTicket = true;
if ($age >= 18 && $hasTicket) {
    echo "Welcome\n";
}
if ($age < 12 || $age > 65) {
    echo "Discount\n";
}
if (!$hasTicket) {
    echo "Buy a ticket\n";
}

lesson.md: `match` compares a value with several options and returns the result of the first option that fits. It compares with `===`. Each option is written as `value => result`, and options end with a comma. Several values can share one result. `default` is used when nothing fits. Without `default`, a value that fits nothing causes an error.

lesson.code:
<?php
$day = 6;
$type = match ($day) {
    1, 2, 3, 4, 5 => "Workday",
    6, 7 => "Weekend",
    default => "Unknown",
};
echo $type, "\n";

lesson.md: Do not confuse `=` with `===`. `$x = 5` stores `5` in `$x`, while `$x === 5` asks whether `$x` is `5`. A condition like `if ($x = 5)` stores the value and is always `true`.

card: `===` same value and type, `==` converts types

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with while, for and foreach, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. A `while` loop runs its block again and again, as long as its condition is `true`. `$count--` subtracts 1 from `$count`, so the condition becomes `false` at some point.

lesson.code:
<?php
$count = 3;
while ($count > 0) {
    echo $count, "\n";
    $count--;
}
echo "Go!\n";

lesson.md: A `for` loop is the usual way to count. Its parentheses hold three parts, separated by semicolons: the start (`$i = 1`), the condition (`$i <= 3`) and the step that runs after each round (`$i++`). The step can also be `$i -= 3` to count down by 3.

lesson.code:
<?php
for ($i = 1; $i <= 3; $i++) {
    echo "Line $i\n";
}
for ($i = 10; $i > 0; $i -= 3) {
    echo $i, "\n";
}

lesson.md: An **array** is a list of values in square brackets, like `["apple", "banana"]`. You learn more about arrays in a later unit. `foreach` goes through every element of an array: `foreach ($fruits as $fruit)` puts each element into `$fruit`, one after the other.
With `foreach ($fruits as $index => $fruit)`, you also get the position of each element. Positions start at `0`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
foreach ($fruits as $fruit) {
    echo "I like $fruit\n";
}
foreach ($fruits as $index => $fruit) {
    echo "$index: $fruit\n";
}
lesson.output:
I like apple
I like banana
I like cherry
0: apple
1: banana
2: cherry

lesson.md: `break` ends the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one. In this example, `continue` skips the even numbers and `break` stops the loop after `7`.

lesson.code:
<?php
for ($i = 1; $i <= 10; $i++) {
    if ($i % 2 === 0) {
        continue;
    }
    if ($i > 7) {
        break;
    }
    echo $i, "\n";
}

lesson.md: If the condition of a loop never becomes `false`, the loop runs forever. This is called an **infinite loop**. Check that something inside the loop changes the condition, for example `$count--`.
Use `foreach` to go through an array, `for` when you know how many rounds you need, and `while` when you do not know it in advance.

card: `break` stops the loop, `continue` skips a round

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions with parameters, default values and types, call them with named arguments and use arrow functions.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can use again and again. You define it with `function`, a name and parentheses for the **parameters**. To call it, write its name and put the values, called **arguments**, in the parentheses.

lesson.code:
<?php
function greet($name) {
    echo "Hello, $name!\n";
}

greet("Ada");
greet("Linus");

lesson.md: `return` sends a value back to the place where the function was called. The function stops there. You can store the returned value in a variable or use it directly in a calculation.

lesson.code:
<?php
function add($a, $b) {
    return $a + $b;
}

$sum = add(2, 3);
echo $sum, "\n";
echo add(10, 20) * 2, "\n";

lesson.md: You can write a type before each parameter, and the **return type** after a colon `:` behind the parentheses. Use `void` when a function returns nothing. A parameter with `=` and a value has a **default value**, so you can leave it out when you call the function.

lesson.code:
<?php
function area(float $width, float $height = 1.0): float {
    return $width * $height;
}

echo area(3, 4), "\n";
echo area(5), "\n";

lesson.md: PHP checks the types when the function runs. If a value does not fit, for example the text `"abc"` for an `int` parameter, PHP stops with a `TypeError`.
You can also pass arguments by the name of their parameter: `size: "L"`. Then the order does not matter, and you can skip parameters that have a default value.

lesson.code:
<?php
function order(string $item, int $count = 1, string $size = "M"): string {
    return "$count x $item ($size)";
}

echo order("Tea"), "\n";
echo order("Coffee", size: "L"), "\n";
echo order(count: 3, item: "Juice"), "\n";
lesson.output:
1 x Tea (M)
1 x Coffee (L)
3 x Juice (M)

lesson.md: An **arrow function** is a short function without a name: `fn($x) => $x * 2`. It returns the value after `=>` without `return`. You can store it in a variable and call it like `$double(4)`. It can use variables from outside, with the value they have when the arrow function is created.

lesson.code:
<?php
$double = fn($x) => $x * 2;
echo $double(4), "\n";

$factor = 3;
$times = fn($x) => $x * $factor;
echo $times(5), "\n";

card: `function f(int $n = 1): string` adds types and a default

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Keep many values in indexed and associative arrays, and use count, in_array, implode, array_map and array_filter.

lesson.md: An **array** keeps many values in one variable. You write the values in square brackets `[ ]`, separated by commas. Each value has an **index**, its position, starting at `0`. `$colors[0]` reads the first element.

lesson.code:
<?php
$colors = ["red", "green", "blue"];
echo $colors[0], "\n";
echo $colors[2], "\n";
$colors[] = "yellow";
$colors[1] = "lime";
echo count($colors), "\n";
echo implode(", ", $colors), "\n";
lesson.output:
red
blue
4
red, lime, blue, yellow

lesson.md: `$colors[] = "yellow"` adds a value to the end of the array. `$colors[1] = "lime"` replaces the element at index `1`. `count` returns the number of elements, and `implode` joins all elements into one string, with the separator you give first.

In an **associative array**, each value has a name, called a **key**, instead of a number. You write `key => value`. Read a value with its key: `$person["name"]`. Inside double quotes, put curly braces around it: `{$person["age"]}`.

lesson.code:
<?php
$person = ["name" => "Ada", "age" => 36];
echo $person["name"], "\n";
$person["city"] = "London";
foreach ($person as $key => $value) {
    echo "$key: $value\n";
}
echo "Age: {$person["age"]}\n";
lesson.output:
Ada
name: Ada
age: 36
city: London
Age: 36

lesson.md: `in_array($value, $array)` returns `true` when the value is in the array. The value must match exactly, including capital and small letters.

lesson.code:
<?php
$fruits = ["apple", "pear", "plum"];
var_dump(in_array("pear", $fruits));
var_dump(in_array("kiwi", $fruits));
if (in_array("plum", $fruits)) {
    echo "We have plums\n";
}

lesson.md: `array_map` calls a function for every element and returns a new array with the results. `array_filter` returns a new array with only the elements for which the function returns `true`. `array_sum` adds up all numbers in an array. Arrow functions are a good fit here.

lesson.code:
<?php
$numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6];
$squares = array_map(fn($n) => $n * $n, $numbers);
echo implode(" ", $squares), "\n";
$even = array_filter($numbers, fn($n) => $n % 2 === 0);
echo implode(" ", $even), "\n";
echo array_sum($numbers), "\n";

lesson.md: The order of the arguments is different: `array_map` takes the function first, but `array_filter` takes the array first. Also, `array_filter` keeps the original indexes of the elements it keeps.
Reading an index or key that does not exist, like `$colors[10]`, gives the warning `Undefined array key`. Use `count` to know how many elements an array has.

units.title: Classes and objects
units.summary: Build your own classes with properties and methods, create objects with new and write short constructors with promotion.

lesson.md: A **class** is a blueprint. It describes data, called **properties**, and functions, called **methods**. From one class you can create many **objects** with the keyword `new`.

lesson.code:
<?php
class Dog {
    public string $name = "Rex";

    public function bark(): string {
        return "Woof!";
    }
}

$dog = new Dog();
echo $dog->name, "\n";
echo $dog->bark(), "\n";

lesson.md: `public` means that code outside the class can use the property or method. `string` is the type of the property. The arrow `->` reads a property or calls a method of an object: `$dog->name` and `$dog->bark()`. By convention, class names start with a capital letter.

The method `__construct` is the **constructor**. It runs automatically when you create an object, and it gets the arguments you pass to `new`. Inside a method, `$this` is the current object, so `$this->title` is the property `title` of this object.

lesson.code:
<?php
class Book {
    public string $title;
    public int $pages;

    public function __construct(string $title, int $pages) {
        $this->title = $title;
        $this->pages = $pages;
    }
}

$book = new Book("Dune", 412);
echo $book->title, " has ", $book->pages, " pages\n";

lesson.md: There is a shorter way. When you write `public` before a constructor parameter, PHP creates the property and stores the argument in it for you. This is called **constructor property promotion**. The body of the constructor can then stay empty: `{}`.

lesson.code:
<?php
class Point {
    public function __construct(
        public int $x,
        public int $y,
    ) {}

    public function describe(): string {
        return "($this->x, $this->y)";
    }
}

$p = new Point(3, 4);
echo $p->describe(), "\n";
$p->x = 10;
echo $p->describe(), "\n";

lesson.md: A `private` property can only be used inside the class. Code outside must call the methods instead. This way, the class controls how its data changes. Here, the only way to change the balance is the method `deposit`.

lesson.code:
<?php
class Account {
    public function __construct(
        private float $balance = 0,
    ) {}

    public function deposit(float $amount): void {
        $this->balance += $amount;
    }

    public function getBalance(): float {
        return $this->balance;
    }
}

$account = new Account(50);
$account->deposit(25);
$account->deposit(10.5);
echo $account->getBalance(), "\n";

lesson.md: Reading a `private` property from outside the class, like `$account->balance`, stops the script with an error. Use a public method such as `getBalance()` instead.
Every `new` creates a separate object with its own properties. If you change `$a->x`, the property `x` of another object `$b` stays the same.

card: `$this` is the current object inside a method
`private` can only be used inside the class
